title.title: A classification of Euclidean Ramsey configurations
title.subtitle: Claim: a finite point set is Ramsey exactly when a tensor condition over its coordinate field holds

plain: Colour space with a few colours: which shapes always show up in one colour? An algebra test now decides

beats.text: Which point sets show up in one colour, at their own scale, in every finite colouring?
The claimed criterion implies any five points on a circle do
So does this kite, though it sits in no symmetric set: a 2012 conjecture falls

steps: Rewrite the points' sphere equation in a tensor square of numbers
No solution there? Then a colouring avoids the shape
A solution? Then Hales–Jewett forces a one-colour copy

achievement.label: Euclidean Ramsey theory: which finite sets are Ramsey?
statement: A \text{ Ramsey} \iff \text{a tensor condition over } F \otimes_{\mathbb Q} F
achievement.context: Refutes the Leader–Russell–Walters characterisation; Graham's spherical conjecture fell days earlier
achievement.note: The criterion is algebraic, not a procedure from numerical coordinates

verify.detail: The classification, five concyclic points, and a 12-point, 50-colour example
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement; we did not build it

voice.text: Colour space with finitely many colours. Which point sets always appear in a single colour?
Ramsey or not comes down to whether one algebra equation has a solution.

sources.quote: every subtransitive set and every set of at most five concyclic points is Ramsey
the non-subtransitive cyclic kites of Leader–Russell–Walters are Ramsey
Leader–Russell–Walters (JCTA 2012, 'Transitive sets in Euclidean Ramsey theory') conjectured Ramsey iff subtransitive
Graham's spherical conjecture had been refuted on September 20, about two weeks before the release went public
deciding it for a given configuration is not obviously algorithmic (paper says it is not a procedure from numerical coordinates)
